```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"ok":false,"error":{"code":"not_initialized","message":"Review guides are missing for owner/repo.","hint":"co-maintainer init owner/repo"},"exitCode":2}
```

In the terminal the message goes to stderr, then the line
`Hint: co-maintainer init owner/repo`, and stdout stays empty. PR review and
remote review put `[error] ` in front of the message, like every other error of
those modes. Local review and PR review hint `init` on your machine. The guides
of a remote review live on the server, so `init` on your machine would not fix
it, and the message names the server instead:

```
[error] Review guides are missing for owner/repo on review.example.com.
Hint: Run co-maintainer init owner/repo on the server at review.example.com.
```

This holds for `review --remote` and for `review --remote --range`. The one
exception is a push to a repository the [GitHub App](github-app.md) already
covers. The App marks that commit's check run as skipped, so the command prints a
notice saying so and exits 0, see [commit watch](commit-watch-review.md).

A repository the server does not know is a different error, `repo_unavailable`,
see [Remote review](remote-review.md#errors-from-the-server).

### What counts as blocking

`reviewBlocking` in `config.json` decides it, and the same rule is used by
local, PR, remote and the automatic GitHub App reviews.

| Value | A finding blocks when |
| ----- | ----- |
| `model` (default) | The model says so. A P0 always blocks, even if the model labeled it otherwise. |
| `severity` | Its severity is P0 or P1. P2 and P3 never block, whatever the model said. |

The default keeps the 0.4.13 behavior. `severity` exists because the model's
own label can move between two reviews of the same code, which flipped the exit
code for the same finding. With `severity` the same finding set always yields
the same exit code, the same `blocking` count in `--json`, and the same GitHub
review type.

```sh
co-maintainer config set --review-blocking=severity
co-maintainer config set --review-blocking=model      # back to the default
```

`CO_MAINTAINER_REVIEW_BLOCKING` overrides it for one environment.

The automatic GitHub App review picks its type from the open findings, with the
same rule as the exit code. With no open blocking finding it approves, and any
non-blocking findings stay as comments on that approval. With an open blocking
finding it requests changes. An approval also clears an earlier "changes
requested" from the App, which a comment-only review could not.

A bot approval counts toward a repository's required approvals, so a pull
request with open non-blocking comments can become mergeable on the App's
approval alone.

## JSON output

With `--json`, stdout is a single JSON object (`schemaVersion` `1`). Fields
include `mode` (`local`, `remote`, or `pr`), `subject`, `summary`, `findings[]`,
`warnings[]`, `usage`, and `durationMs`. Every mode includes `revision`, which
counts the files and says which of them the model received in full, see
[Large diffs](#large-diffs). Local and remote runs also include `codegraph`
state. `usage.tools` counts the tool calls, see [Tool usage](#tool-usage). `extensions` is always an array, empty when nothing is registered, and
every finding has `extensionId`, which is `null` for an AI finding, see
[Extensions](#extensions). `subject.intent` is there only when the review was
given an [intent](#intent). Errors with `--json` are JSON on stdout as well.

Flag details per mode: [Local review](local-review.md), [Remote review](remote-review.md),
[PR review](local-pr-review.md).

## GitHub output

`--output=github` prints the findings as GitHub workflow annotations and writes a
table to the job summary, for a run inside GitHub Actions. It works in all three
modes and cannot be combined with `--json`.

- Each finding that is still open becomes one command on stdout, `::error` when it
  blocks and `::warning` when it does not, with its file, line span and a short
  title. A finding closed since the last review is not annotated.
- When `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` is set, a table of every finding, the cost and the
  time is appended to it. An unknown cost reads `cost unknown` with the reason.
- The exit code is the same as without the flag, so a blocking finding fails the
  step.
- Nothing else goes to stdout in this mode. Every finding is one escaped line, so
  text from a pull request can never start a workflow command of its own.

GitHub shows at most ten errors and ten warnings per step. When there are more,
one notice says how many were left out, and the job summary lists all of them.
[CI](ci.md) shows it inside a workflow.

## Human output

Without `--json`, all three modes print the **same** format. Only the header
names the mode, because the subject differs:

```
co-maintainer review · owner/repo · my-branch
4 files · +12 −3 · guide built 2026-09-15 · codegraph used

New (1)
  • src/app.ts:16-18  [P1 · blocking] the gate ignores its threshold
    A violation exactly at the threshold passes.

Still open (1)
  • src/util.ts:4  [P2 · non-blocking] the helper ignores its argument

Closed (1)
  ✓ src/old.ts:9  [P2 · non-blocking] the dead branch

Summary: 1 new · 1 open · 1 closed · 2 blocking
Tools: 11 calls · 18,240 characters
```

Findings are grouped `Closed`, `Still open`, `New`, each labeled with the same
`blocking` decision the exit code uses. The header names the real guide build
date (`guide unknown` only when no guide timestamp can be read) and the state
the run actually reached: `codegraph used`, `codegraph disabled`, or
`codegraph unavailable`: the last one when codegraph was requested but could
not be prepared, which is also what `--json` reports. When a file did not reach
the model in full, a `Coverage:` line follows the summary, see
[Large diffs](#where-the-result-says-it). For the `Tools:` line, see
[Tool usage](#tool-usage).

The severity legend and the "If you'd like me to explain it in more detail,
please ask." sentence are **not** in terminal output: a terminal has nobody to
ask, and the legend is fixed noise. Both stay in the GitHub review comment,
which is a different reader.

## How findings are produced

The model is asked for a JSON object, not for prose. For each finding it returns
the severity, whether it blocks, the path and line span, the symbol, a title, the
explanation, and an optional replacement. `co-maintainer` renders the Markdown
from that object, so a finding's boundaries are never guessed from the model's
wording. The JSON schema is sent as structured output in the provider's own format
when the provider accepts it. A provider that rejects the combination gets one request
without the schema, and the prompt also asks for a fenced JSON block.

If the answer is not usable JSON, the request is retried once and then, if it
still fails, the older Markdown parser reads it. That parser accepts the em
dash or `:` as the heading separator, so answers written before this change (and
carry-over records saved by `0.4.13`) keep working. The `--json` output and the
human output are both built from the same parsed findings, so they can never
disagree.

## Before any review

| Check | Why |
| ----- | --- |
| [`init`](init.md) or [`sync`](sync.md) on your laptop | Required for local and PR review |
| An [AI provider](providers.md) for local and PR review, with both models saved | AI runs on your machine, and no model is picked for you |
| [Remote setup](remote-review.md) for `--remote` | Host, token, repo already inited on the server |

---

Source: https://co-maintainer.com/docs/local-review.md

# Local review

Review **staged, unstaged, and untracked** files in your git clone against a
base branch. AI and guides run on **your machine**, with the
[AI provider](providers.md) you saved.

Overview: [`review`](review.md).

## Before you run

| Check | Why |
| ----- | --- |
| Run from the repo root (or a subdirectory with a git root) | Review needs a working tree |
| `origin` or `upstream` points at GitHub (or use `--repo=owner/repo`) | Maps the clone to guides for that repo |
| [`init`](init.md) / [`sync`](sync.md) for that `owner/repo` | `SKILL.md` and review guides on disk |
| A provider key in `set`, `--token=`, or `--env=PATH` | Local review uses your [provider](providers.md) |
| Clean enough git state | Conflicts or broken git state can fail collection |

## Usage

```sh
cd your/clone
co-maintainer review
co-maintainer review --json
co-maintainer review --fresh
co-maintainer review --to-branch=main --sync-before-review
```

## Parameters

| Flag | Meaning |
| ------ | ----- |
| `--json` | One JSON document on stdout, no prompts |
| `--disable-codegraph` | Skip codegraph tools (default is on) |
| `--allow-tool-install` | Install pinned codegraph without a prompt when missing |
| `--fresh` | Ignore carry-over from the previous local review on this branch |
| `--intent-file=PATH` | What the change is for, from a file or `-` for standard input. Context only, read into the `WORKSPACE` block, see [Intent](review.md#intent) |
| `--with=PATH[@BRANCH]` | Read another checkout's changes as context, up to 5, see [Companions](companions.md) |
| `--diagram-runtime`, `--plantuml-server`, `--plantuml-output-format` | The diagram language of the review, see [Diagrams](review.md#diagrams) |
| `--to-branch=<name>` | Base branch for the diff (default: remote default branch) |
| `--branch=<name>` | Branch name when HEAD is detached |
| `--repo=owner/repo` | Override GitHub remote detection |
| `--sync-before-review` | Run [`sync`](sync.md) before reviewing (requires `gh`) |
| `--include-extension-markdowns` | With `--json`, keep each extension's Markdown, which is empty otherwise |
| `--debug` | Verbose logs on stderr |
| `--log-time` | Print timing per phase |

Registered [extensions](extensions.md) run in a local review too, in your working
directory, and their findings join the result.

Do not pass `owner/repo` or a PR number. That selects [PR review](local-pr-review.md)
instead.

## Codegraph

Local review uses codegraph to follow calls between files. On the first run the
pinned build is usually missing, and co-maintainer asks before installing it (see
[Caching](caching.md) for the per-version tools directory). The question names
the package, where it comes from, what it is for, the approximate download size,
and the exact install directory:

```
co-maintainer uses codegraph 1.6.0 (@colbymchenry/codegraph from npm, ~250 MB) to follow calls between files while reviewing.
Install it into <tools dir>/codegraph/1.6.0 (your global PATH is not touched)? [y/N]
```

The question is only asked when **both** stdin and stdout are a terminal and
`CI` is unset. With a closed stdin (`</dev/null`), a piped output, or `CI=1`, it
is skipped and review continues without codegraph, printing one line:

```
[codegraph] codegraph 1.6.0 is not installed, reviewing without it. Pass --allow-tool-install to install it, or --disable-codegraph to skip this notice.
```

Pass `--allow-tool-install` to install without a prompt, or
`--disable-codegraph` to skip the check entirely. Neither CI jobs nor pipelines
can hang on the question. Full details, including the install table and the
version-resolution order, are in [Codegraph](codegraph.md).

## Carry-over

Repeated `co-maintainer review` on the same repo root and branch reuses prior
findings (closed / still open / new) via [cache](caching.md). Use `--fresh` to
start clean. If the cache cannot be read or written, review continues with a
`carry_over_unavailable` warning.

Carry-over never replaces the review. Every run scans the whole diff for new
violations **and** re-checks the previous findings. A finding that is still open
is reported as such rather than suppressing a new one nearby.

A change too large for one review is covered over the next runs. A file the model
did not receive is sent again, so run `review` again and read the `Coverage:`
line, see [Large diffs](review.md#large-diffs).

When a guide is rebuilt (`init` / `sync`) after your last review on this branch,
that review's verdicts were made against rules that no longer exist. The next
review therefore starts fresh on its own (no `--fresh` needed), so a stale
finding cannot hide a violation the new guide would catch.

## Developers

```sh
npm run review-local-e2e
```

Temporary worktree, `CM_FAKE_AI=1`, optional `CM_FAKE_REVIEW_FILE`.

---

Source: https://co-maintainer.com/docs/remote-review.md

# Remote review

Same **local git diff** as [local review](local-review.md), but **review guides
come from the server**. The team runs [`init`](init.md) / [`sync`](sync.md)
once on [`serve`](serve.md). Developers clone, set host and token, and run
`review --remote` without maintaining their own guide cache.

The model runs on the server as part of that path. Codegraph tools (when enabled)
and [`search-non-code`](review.md#searching-docs-and-configuration) still run on
the laptop and return results through the tool bridge. A server older than
0.7.10 ignores the search tool. Your own MCP servers can join as
[client tools](#your-own-mcp-servers-as-client-tools) when the server allows it.

Overview: [`review`](review.md). Requires [`serve`](serve.md) and the
[dashboard](dashboard.md).

## Before you run

| Check | Why |
| ----- | --- |
| Server running `co-maintainer serve` | Hosts remote review API and shared repo context |
| Repo added on the dashboard with **init** / **sync** | Guides live on the server for everyone |
| **Settings → Remote review** token (`cmr_…`) | Bearer auth for the CLI |
| `co-maintainer set --remote-host=... --remote-token=...` on the laptop | CLI knows where to connect (or pass `--remote-host=` / `--remote-token=` for one run) |
| Git clone with the same diff you would use for local review | Command is still `review --remote` with no PR number |

You do **not** need a local `init` / `sync` for that repo if the server
already has it.

PR review (`owner/repo` + number) **cannot** use `--remote`.

## Usage

```sh
co-maintainer set --remote-host=https://your-server --remote-token=cmr_...
cd your/clone
co-maintainer review --remote
co-maintainer review --remote --json --disable-codegraph
# One-off, without saving host and token to the config:
co-maintainer review --remote --remote-host=https://your-server --remote-token=cmr_...
# Or by environment, which keeps the token off the command line:
CM_REMOTE_HOST=https://your-server CM_REMOTE_TOKEN=cmr_... co-maintainer review --remote
```

To run it on every pull request from a workflow, see [CI](ci.md).

## Parameters

Same as [local review](local-review.md) for diff and output flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
| ------ | ----- |
| `--json` | JSON on stdout |
| `--disable-codegraph` | Skip local codegraph |
| `--allow-tool-install` | Allow codegraph install without a prompt |
| `--fresh` | No carry-over from a prior remote run |
| `--intent-file=PATH` | What the change is for, from a file or `-` for standard input. Context only, see [The intent file](#the-intent-file). Not with `--range` |
| `--with=PATH[@BRANCH]` | Send another checkout's changes as context, up to 5, see [Companions](companions.md#remote-review). Not with `--range` |
| `--to-branch=<name>` | Diff base branch |
| `--branch=<name>` | Branch when HEAD is detached |
| `--repo=owner/repo` | Override remote detection |
| `--remote-host=<url>` | Override the configured host for this run (needs `--remote`) |
| `--remote-token=<token>` | Override the configured token for this run (needs `--remote`) |
| `--remote-byok` | Send your own AI key with this review, see [your own key](#your-own-ai-key) |
| `--no-remote-byok` | Do not send it, even when `remote-byok-default` is on |
| `--include-extension-markdowns` | With `--json`, keep each extension's Markdown, which is empty otherwise |
| `--output=github` | Print GitHub annotations and write the job summary, see [CI](ci.md). Cannot be used with `--json` |
| `--debug` | Verbose stderr |
| `--log-time` | Phase timings |

The codegraph question, and the conditions under which co-maintainer skips it,
are the same as [local review](local-review.md#codegraph).

Not supported with `--remote`: `--sync-before-review` (run
[`sync`](sync.md) on the server instead), and `--diagram-runtime`,
`--plantuml-server` and `--plantuml-output-format`. Each is refused with exit
code 2, because the server reviews with the diagram settings saved for the
repository, see [Configuration](configuration.md#diagram-settings).

The server reviews with its own provider, models and key, so `--ai`,
`--token`, `--ai-key`, `--low-model`, `--high-model`, `--auth`, `--github-pat`
and `--improve-matrix` are refused the same way, and so is any flag a remote
review does not know, a typo included. `--debug` and `--log-time` print one
stderr line per call to the server, with its status and time.

The repository's exclude pattern applies to a remote review and a push review
the same as to a pull request review: the matching files are left out and the
prompt says so.

## Token scope

A remote token is not tied to one repository: any token can review, and read
the guides of, every active repository on the server. Hand a token only to
people you trust with all of them, and revoke a leaked one from **Settings →
Remote review tokens**.

## Reading the server's guides

The same token that authorizes a review also reads the guides the server holds,
so you can inspect what your review will be judged against without downloading
anything:

```sh
co-maintainer view owner/repo --remote            # every guide, with headers
co-maintainer view owner/repo review-guide --remote   # one guide, raw
co-maintainer view owner/repo --list --remote     # file, size, build date
co-maintainer view owner/repo --sources --remote  # the instruction rules and their source lines
```

The output is the same format as a local `co-maintainer view`, with the same
`--list`, single-guide and header behavior. Only the source differs. `--path`
is local-only and is refused with `--remote`, because the directory belongs to
the machine you are on. A rejected token prints the same Settings hint
`review --remote` prints.

## Your own AI key

By default the server's provider and key pay for a remote review. A server can
also let you bring your own key (BYOK), so the review is billed to you and not to
the server. The server still chooses the provider and the models, only the key is
yours. See [AI providers](providers.md).

### From the command line

```sh
co-maintainer config set remote-byok YOUR_KEY          # save the key once
co-maintainer review --remote --remote-byok            # send it with this review
co-maintainer config set remote-byok-default on        # send it every time
co-maintainer review --remote --no-remote-byok         # but not this time
CM_REMOTE_BYOK=YOUR_KEY co-maintainer review --remote --remote-byok
```

`--remote-byok` only works with `--remote`. The key comes from `CM_REMOTE_BYOK`
first, then from the `remote-byok` config value. With `remote-byok-default on` the
flag is not needed, and `--no-remote-byok` turns it off for one run. Before it
sends anything, the CLI prints `Using your own key with the server's provider:`
followed by the provider's name.

The CLI never falls back to the server's key when you asked for your own. Each of
these stops the run with exit code 2 before the diff is sent:

| Message | Why | What to do |
| ------- | --- | ---------- |
| `No BYOK key is set.` | `--remote-byok` with no key anywhere | `co-maintainer config set remote-byok <key>`, or set `CM_REMOTE_BYOK` |
| `This server (version X) does not support your own key.` | The server predates the feature and would ignore the key, so the CLI refuses to rely on it | Upgrade the server, or run without `--remote-byok` |
| `This server does not accept your own key.` | The server's policy is `off` | Run without `--remote-byok` |
| `This server requires your own key.` | The server's policy is `require` and the run did not send one | `co-maintainer review --remote --remote-byok` |

If the host starts with `http://` and is not `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `::1`,
the CLI warns on stderr that anyone on the network path can read the key, then
carries on. Use `https://`. Both stderr lines are
left out with `--json`.

### On the server

The policy is a server setting, `off`, `allow` or `require`:

| Policy | A review without a key | A review with a key |
| ------ | ---------------------- | ------------------- |
| `off` (the default) | Uses the server's key | Refused with 403: `This server does not accept your own key.` |
| `allow` | Uses the server's key | Uses your key |
| `require` | Refused with 403: `This server requires your own key. Run with --remote-byok.` | Uses your key |

Set it under **Settings**, **Remote review**, **Client key policy (BYOK)**, with
`co-maintainer set --remote-byok-policy=allow`, or with the `CM_REMOTE_BYOK_POLICY`
environment variable. The variable wins over the saved value, so a hosted server
keeps its policy. The handshake tells the CLI which policy is in force and which
provider the server uses. It never includes a key or a model.

### What happens to the key

- It is kept in the server's memory for that one review. It is removed when the
  review finishes, is canceled, or is replaced by a newer submit.
- It is never written to `app.db`, to the cache, to the config, or to a log or a
  job log. A test searches the raw database file and every log for a known key
  after a full review.
- If the server restarts while your review is waiting, the key is gone with it.
  The review ends with `Your key was not kept across a server restart. Submit the
  review again.` and the server's own key is never used instead.
- If the provider refuses the key, the error says so and names your key:
  `The AI provider rejected your own key.` Other provider failures are reported
  as what they are.

### Cost

A review sent with a key is recorded as billed to the key's owner. The dashboard
keeps it out of the server's own spend. A total reads `$1.23 + $0.40 BYOK`, the
server's cost first and what clients paid with their own keys after the plus
sign. See [Cost](cost.md).

## Extensions

A remote review runs the [extensions](extensions.md) registered on `serve`, as
review type `remote`, and the registrations on your own machine do not run. The
extension has no working directory with your checkout, because the checkout is
on your machine. Its findings, verdict and cost come back in the result.

## MCP servers

A remote review offers the model the tools of the
[MCP servers](review.md#mcp-servers) the server has for the repository, set on
the `serve` host with `co-maintainer set --repo=owner/repo --mcp-config=...`.
They run on the server, as its extensions do. Their results stay on the server:
the copied-passage check runs there before the result comes back, and the
`mcp_*` and `private_text_removed` warnings come back with it.

### Your own MCP servers as client tools

The MCP servers in your own `config.json` for the repository can take part too,
when the server allows it. Your CLI starts them, declares their tools to the
server, and runs each call the server's model makes, on your machine.

- **The server decides.** The policy is `remoteClientToolsPolicy`, `off` by
  default or `on`. Set it on the `serve` host with
  `co-maintainer set --remote-client-tools-policy=on`, or with the
  `CM_REMOTE_CLIENT_TOOLS_POLICY` environment variable, which wins over the
  saved value, as the [BYOK policy](#on-the-server) does.
- **The handshake says it.** A server from 0.7.12 lists `client-tools` among its
  features and sends its policy. With `on`, the CLI starts your servers and the
  submit's `capabilities.tools` carries each tool's name, description and
  parameters. With `off`, or on an older server, the CLI starts none, declares
  nothing, and adds the warning `client_tools_refused`. The review runs. An
  older CLI with a newer server sends tool names only, and nothing changes.
- **Names.** The model sees your tool `mcp-<server>-<tool>` as
  `client-<server>-<tool>` in lowercase, with any character other than a letter,
  a digit or a dash turned into a dash, for example `client-tracker-get-issue`.
  The same rules as on your machine apply first: only the tools in `tools`, and
  never one the MCP server marks as not read-only.
- **The server's limits.** At most 16 declared tools, 64 KB for all of them
  together, at most 16 KB per
  declaration, and a name of 2 to 64 lowercase letters, digits or dashes that
  starts with a letter and is not a name of the server's own tools
  (`codegraph-*`, `search-non-code`, `read-full-diff`, `read-mermaid-syntaxes`,
  `mcp-*`). Each declaration it leaves out gives a `client_tools_refused`
  warning that names it.
- **Results.** Every result goes through the server's
  [tool limits](review.md#tool-limits) like any other tool's, behind the line
  that says it is data from outside the repository. The server takes at most
  40,000 characters of one result from the CLI. Every result is private: the
  prompt says so, and the server runs the copied-passage check on them before
  the result comes back.
- `CM_MCP_DISABLED=1` on your machine starts none of your servers.

## The intent file

`review --remote --intent-file=PATH` sends the text with the review. What it is
and how the result records it is on [Review](review.md#intent). On a server the
text comes from a client, so it is treated as untrusted.

- **The cap.** The client checks the repository's `reviewSystemPromptMaxChars`
  from its own config (8000 by default) before it sends. The server applies its
  own cap to the trimmed text again. A longer text is refused with 400,
  `revision.description: must be at most N characters (got M)`, and the client
  says `--intent-file was refused by the server:` followed by that. A description
  over 200,000 characters is refused with `revision.description: too long`.
- **A refused submit changes nothing.** The branch's running review and its
  carry-over stay as they were.
- **An older server.** The handshake lists `intent` among its features. A client
  that does not find it does not send the text and adds the warning
  `intent_unsupported`, which says "This server (version X) does not support an
  intent, so the review ran without one." The review runs. An older client with
  a newer server sends nothing, and nothing changes.
- **What the server keeps.** Only the trimmed text, in the job's input row until
  the review ends, the same as the diff. It is never written to a log or a
  result. The client sets `subject.intent` itself, so a server cannot change it.
  The characters U+2028 and U+2029 reach the prompt as a newline escape.
- **Push reviews** (`--range`) take no intent, and the server ignores a
  description sent with one.

## Companions

`review --remote --with=PATH[@BRANCH]` builds each companion's diff on your
machine and sends it with the review. A server that lists `companions` among
its features reads them, takes at most 500,000 characters of their patches in
total, and asks your machine to search a companion. An older server gets none,
and the run warns `companions_unsupported`. See
[Companions](companions.md#remote-review).

## Errors from the server

When the server refuses the handshake, the code tells the cases apart. Each of
these exits with code 2 and writes no job.

| Code | Text | Hint |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| `not_initialized` | `Review guides are missing for owner/repo on <host>.` | `Run co-maintainer init owner/repo on the server at <host>.` |
| `repo_unavailable` | `The server at <host> does not have owner/repo available for review.` | `Check the owner/repo name, or add the repository on that server first.` |
| `remote_handshake_failed` | The server's own text, with control characters removed | |

`repo_unavailable` is the same answer for a repository the server does not know
and one that is switched off. `remote_handshake_failed` stays for every other
refusal, and for a refusal that carries no error code. `review --remote --range`
gets `not_initialized` from the server's refusal of the push, with the same
hint. Everything else about the two codes is on
[Review](review.md#a-repository-without-guides).

## Limits

- Submit body size is capped (handshake `limits.maxBodyBytes`).
- Concurrent remote reviews per token and job queue limits in dashboard Settings.
- If sync stops longer than `remoteSyncTimeoutSeconds`, the server cancels the job.
  While the CLI runs the server's tool calls it keeps sending a sync with no
  results, at the poll interval and at least three times per timeout, so a slow
  tool batch is not taken for a client that went away.
- The server plans a large diff, and a file it dropped is sent again in your next
  `review --remote`. See [Large diffs](review.md#large-diffs).

## Security

- Tokens are hashed at rest. Treat `cmr_…` like a password.
- A key you send travels with the request. Use an `https://` host, and see
  [What happens to the key](#what-happens-to-the-key).
- Deactivating or deleting a token cancels in-flight remote reviews for that token.
- Only your **diff** leaves the machine. The CLI shows a one-time notice per host.

---

Source: https://co-maintainer.com/docs/ci.md

# CI (GitHub Action)

Run [remote review](remote-review.md) on every pull request from a workflow. The
findings show up as annotations on the changed files, a table lands in the job
summary, and the step turns red when a finding blocks.

The action needs a server that already runs `co-maintainer serve` with the
repository added, and a remote review token from its dashboard. It sends the
diff of the pull request to that server, the same way `review --remote` does
from a laptop.

## Set it up

1. On the dashboard open **Settings**, **Remote review tokens** and create a
   token for CI.
2. In the GitHub repository open **Settings**, **Secrets and variables**,
   **Actions**, and add two secrets. `CO_MAINTAINER_HOST` holds the URL of the
   server and `CO_MAINTAINER_REMOTE_TOKEN` holds the token. Do not name it
   `CO_MAINTAINER_TOKEN`: that name is the AI key variable of the CLI, and a
   local review step that read it would send the remote token to the AI
   provider.
3. Add a workflow:

```yaml
name: co-maintainer
on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

# A new push to the pull request replaces the run still going for the last.
concurrency:
  group: co-maintainer-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: GroophyLifefor/co-maintainer@v0
        with:
          remote-host: ${{ secrets.CO_MAINTAINER_HOST }}
          remote-token: ${{ secrets.CO_MAINTAINER_REMOTE_TOKEN }}
```

Without the `concurrency` block an older run still waiting is replaced on the
server too: it ends with a notice and exit code 0, never as a failure. A
pull request review fails with exit code 3 after `review-timeout-minutes`
(30 by default), because the review needs the job to answer it. A server
failure, such as the AI provider failing or a stopped review, is exit code 3
too, so a retry can tell it apart from a wrong workflow (exit code 2).

`fetch-depth: 0` gives the action the history it needs to find where the pull
request branched off. Without it the action fetches what is missing, which is
slower.

## Inputs

| Input | Required | Default | What it does |
| ----- | -------- | ------- | ------------ |
| `remote-host` | yes | none | URL of your server, for example `https://review.example.com` |
| `remote-token` | yes | none | The remote review token. Pass it as a secret |
| `remote-byok` | no | empty | Your own AI key, see [your own key](#your-own-ai-key) |
| `to-branch` | no | the pull request base branch | The branch the pull request merges into |
| `version` | no | the version at the action's own commit | The co-maintainer version to run |
| `node-version` | no | `24` | The Node.js version to run it with |
| `timeout-minutes` | no | `10` | On a push, how long to wait for the review, see [review pushes](#review-pushes-commit-watch) |
| `review-timeout-minutes` | no | `30` | On a pull request, how long the review may take before the step fails with exit code 3 |

Inputs are never removed or renamed within `v0`. A new input is only ever added,
with a default that keeps the old behavior.

## What you see

- **Annotations.** Each finding that is still open is an error when it blocks
  and a warning when it does not. They appear on the **Files changed** tab and
  in the run's annotation list. GitHub shows at most ten errors and ten
  warnings per step, so when there are more the action adds one notice that
  says how many were left out.
- **Job summary.** A table of every finding with its severity, state and
  location, the cost of the review, and how long it took, a push review
  included. An unknown cost reads `cost unknown` with the reason, never `$0`.
  The warnings the terminal would print, such as a stale guide or an MCP
  server that failed, follow as a list and as warning annotations, and a
  review that ran without the call graph says so.
- **Exit status.** The step fails when a finding that is still open blocks,
  the same rule as `review` on the command line. A finding a later round
  closed no longer counts.
- **Extensions.** A finding from an [extension](extensions.md) that has a
  location is annotated with its `[P2 · blocking] · extension: name` label, inside
  the same ten per level. The job summary lists every extension finding and adds
  each extension's Markdown. The summary is capped at 1 MiB, and when it would
  pass that, the longest Markdown is replaced with "Not added to the job summary
  because of the length limit." until it fits.

Nothing else goes to the step's output in this mode, so a finding can never
write a workflow command of its own. See [`review`](review.md) for the
`--output=github` option the action uses.

## Choose which pull requests get reviewed

The action reviews the diff it is given. The server's
[review policy](dashboard.md) decides which pull requests its GitHub App reviews,
and it does not apply here, because a remote review looks at a diff and not at a
pull request. Choose in the workflow instead:

```yaml
    # Skip drafts.
    if: github.event.pull_request.draft == false

    # Skip a bot.
    if: github.actor != 'dependabot[bot]'

    # Only pull requests a maintainer labeled.
    if: contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'needs-review')

    # Only people with a stake in the repository.
    if: contains(fromJSON('["OWNER","MEMBER","COLLABORATOR"]'), github.event.pull_request.author_association)
```

## Review pushes (commit watch)

The same action reviews a push when the workflow runs on `push`. It sends the
diff from the commit before the push to the commit after it. This is
[commit watch](commit-watch-review.md).

```yaml
name: co-maintainer commit watch
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: GroophyLifefor/co-maintainer@v0
        with:
          remote-host: ${{ secrets.CO_MAINTAINER_HOST }}
          remote-token: ${{ secrets.CO_MAINTAINER_REMOTE_TOKEN }}
```

On a push the step never fails because of a finding. Findings are warnings, and
after `timeout-minutes` the step ends green with a notice while the review
finishes on the server. It fails when the server cannot be reached, the token
is refused, or the repository is not initialized and no GitHub App could give
the commit a skipped check run. The action runs
`review --remote --range=<before>..<after>`, which you can run from any other
CI the same way.

## Pull requests from forks

GitHub does not give repository secrets to a workflow started by a pull request
from a fork. The action then sees an empty `remote-token`, stops, and the step
turns red with this message:

```text
remote-token is empty. Pull requests from forks do not receive repository
secrets, so this step cannot run for them.
```

That is on purpose. A quiet skip would look like a clean review. If you would
rather not see red on fork pull requests, skip the job for them:

```yaml
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
```

Do not switch the trigger to `pull_request_target` and check out the fork's code
to get around this. That runs untrusted code with your secrets.

## Pin a version

| You write | What runs | When it changes |
| --------- | --------- | --------------- |
| `@v0` | The newest stable release | On every stable release, on its own |
| `@v0.5.1` | That release | Never |
| A full commit SHA | That exact commit | Never |

The action runs the co-maintainer version that matches its own commit, so
pinning the action pins the tool too. Use `@v0.5.1` or a SHA when a workflow
must not change without a pull request. Beta releases are never reached through
`@v0`.

## Your own AI key

If the server allows it, pass your own key and the review is billed to you and
not to the server. See [remote review](remote-review.md) for the server side of
this.

```yaml
      - uses: GroophyLifefor/co-maintainer@v0
        with:
          remote-host: ${{ secrets.CO_MAINTAINER_HOST }}
          remote-token: ${{ secrets.CO_MAINTAINER_REMOTE_TOKEN }}
          remote-byok: ${{ secrets.OPENROUTER_API_KEY }}
```

The key goes to the tool by environment variable, never on a command line, and
both the token and the key are masked in the log. The server answers with an
error and does not fall back to its own key when it does not accept yours.
This holds for a push review too: the key goes with the push, the review is
marked as billed to you, and a server that requires your key refuses a push
without one. A server older than 0.7.20 cannot take your key for a push, and
the run says so instead of letting the server pay.
Use an `https://` host. The key travels with the request.

## Environment variables

Outside the action the same settings can be given to the CLI by environment:
`CM_REMOTE_HOST`, `CM_REMOTE_TOKEN` and `CM_REMOTE_BYOK`. A flag wins over the
environment, and the environment wins over the saved config. An empty value
counts as not set.

## When it fails

| Message | Cause |
| ------- | ----- |
| `remote-token is empty` | The secret is missing, misspelled, or a fork pull request |
| `Could not fetch the base branch` | `to-branch` names a branch that does not exist on `origin` |
| `This server does not accept your own key` | The server's BYOK policy is `off` |
| `This server requires your own key` | The server's BYOK policy is `require`, add `remote-byok` |

More in [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

---

Source: https://co-maintainer.com/docs/review-policy.md

# Review policy

A review policy decides which pull requests the [GitHub App](github-app.md) reviews
on its own, which ones wait until a maintainer asks, and which are never
reviewed. It runs in [`serve`](serve.md) when a webhook arrives. You set it per
repository in the [dashboard](dashboard.md), and for new repositories as a
server default.

The policy is about the App's reviews. A [remote review](remote-review.md) from
a laptop or from [CI](ci.md) looks at a diff, not at a pull request, so it does
not apply it.

## Three actions

| Action | What happens to a pull request |
| ------ | ------------------------------ |
| Review | It is reviewed automatically |
| Wait for a request | It is left alone until a maintainer [asks](#asking-for-a-review) |
| Do not review | It is never reviewed, and asking does not change that |

## Templates

| Template | What it does |
| -------- | ------------ |
| Everyone | Every pull request is reviewed, except drafts and pull requests by bots |
| Trusted authors, automatic | Owners, members and collaborators are reviewed. Everyone else waits for a request. Drafts and bots are skipped |
| Only when requested | Nothing is reviewed until a maintainer asks |
| Custom rules | Your own list of rules, see below |
| Simple switches | The three on and off switches a repository had before policies existed, see [Existing repositories](#existing-repositories) |

## Rules

A policy is an ordered list of rules. For each pull request the first rule whose
conditions all hold decides the action. When no rule holds, the last setting,
**Any other pull request**, decides. A rule can test:

| Condition | Matches when |
| --------- | ------------ |
| Author | The author's relation to the repository is one of the ones you tick |
| Opened from a fork | The head branch lives in another repository, or in none because the fork was deleted |
| Is a draft | The pull request is a draft, or is not |
| Is by a bot | The author is a bot account, or is not |
| Labels | The pull request has at least one of the labels, compared without regard to case |
| Target branch | The pull request merges into one of the branches, by exact name |
| Changed lines | Additions plus deletions are within a minimum and a maximum |

The author's relation is GitHub's own `author_association`:

| Value | Meaning |
| ----- | ------- |
| `OWNER` | Owns the repository |
| `MEMBER` | Belongs to the organization that owns it |
| `COLLABORATOR` | Was invited to the repository |
| `CONTRIBUTOR` | Has had a commit merged before |
| `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR` | First contribution to this repository |
| `FIRST_TIMER` | First contribution anywhere on GitHub |
| `NONE` | No relation |

A rule that asks about something GitHub did not send never matches.

## Asking for a review

A pull request that waits, or one that no rule reviews, can be started three ways:

- **The request label.** Add `co-maintainer:review` to the pull request. Adding a
  label already needs triage rights, so nothing else is checked.
- **The request comment.** Comment `/co-maintainer review` as the first words of
  a comment on the pull request. Only people in the allowed set can ask, which is
  owners, members and collaborators unless you change it.
- **Review now.** On the dashboard, a pull request that is waiting shows a
  **Review now** button on the Activity page, under **Pull requests we
  skipped**. Whoever is signed in is already allowed to ask, and the button ignores
  the round limit.

When a label or comment request starts a review, the App reacts with an eyes
emoji on the comment or the pull request, so the person who asked can see it was
picked up.

A request never overrides **Do not review**. If a rule skips the pull request, a
request is refused and the reason is recorded.

GitHub sends no fork, target branch or size with a comment, so a **comment**
request is checked again when the review starts and the pull request has been
fetched. If a rule about those three skips it, or it is over the size limit, the
review does not run and no eyes reaction is added.

### What a request covers

| Setting | Covers |
| ------- | ------ |
| Only the commit it was made on | Each new push waits for a new request |
| Every later push to the pull request | After the first review, every push is reviewed |

Comments and reviews on a waiting pull request do not start a review either. The
second setting is the one that carries an earlier request forward.

### Skipping a failed review

A review that fails ends its check run as failed, which blocks the merge where
the check is required. Two comments get past it:

| Comment | When it works | What it does |
| ------- | ------------- | ------------ |
| `/co-maintainer skip-this-commit` | Only when the review of the latest commit failed | A new check run for that commit ends as skipped, and the failed note says the review was skipped. The next commit is reviewed again |
| `/co-maintainer skip-this-pr` | Any time | Reviews are off for this pull request. A review that is running stops and posts nothing. The current commit and every later one get a check run that ends as skipped |
| `/co-maintainer review` | Any time | As above. On a pull request turned off with `skip-this-pr` it also turns reviews back on, and the policy decides what happens next |

A skipped check lets a required check pass without claiming a review happened.
The repository owner may always use the two skip comments. Anyone else only
when **Who else can skip a failed review or turn reviews off** in the
dashboard, or `skippers` in the policy, lists their relation to the
repository. A comment from anyone else is ignored, with no reply and no
reaction.

### When the server is down

The skip comments are read by the server, so they need it running. While it is
down, a **Request changes** review from the App still blocks the merge where
an approving review is required. GitHub's own **Dismiss review** gets past it
with no server:

1. Open the pull request and find the App's review on the **Conversation** tab.
2. Open the review's **...** menu and choose **Dismiss review**.
3. Write why, for example "co-maintainer is down", and confirm.

Anyone with write access to the repository can dismiss a review, unless branch
protection limits dismissals to listed people or teams. The dismissal and its
message stay on the pull request. When the server is back, it also catches up
on its own: a pull request pushed to while it was down gets a review of the new
commit, see [`serve`: Updating](serve.md#updating).

A check run the App left in progress or failed is not cleared by a dismissal.
Where that check is required, wait for the server, or have someone allowed to
bypass branch protection merge.

### Closing a finding

The owner has the last word on a finding, the model does not have to agree. A
reply of `/co-maintainer dismiss` in a finding's thread, with an optional
reason after it, closes that finding as dismissed: accepted risk, will not fix.
The same people who may skip may dismiss, and a comment from anyone else is
ignored. The bot answers in the thread, and the finding is not raised again
while its lines stay the same. The dashboard's **Findings** list has the same
**Close** button, and **Reopen** opens a dismissed or withdrawn finding again.
Each one goes to the audit log with its reason.

Asking in plain words works too. When someone who may dismiss replies in a
finding's thread that it is wrong or asks to close it, the bot closes it, even
if it still reads the code the other way. It says so in one sentence and asks
what the problem with the finding was. The answer to that question goes to the
audit log as feedback on the closed finding. When someone else asks, the bot
says a maintainer can close it and leaves it open.

When the bot agrees in a reply that a finding was wrong, it withdraws it. When
a withdrawn or dismissed finding was the last blocking one, the review asked for
changes, and the pull request is still on the commit that review read, the bot
approves that commit with a fixed text, without an AI call. Otherwise the next
round decides.

### Comment only

**How the review is posted** in a repository's settings, `--review-event` with
`set --repo`, or the server default under **Settings**, **Review defaults**:

| Value | What the App posts |
| ----- | ------------------ |
| `auto` | Approve, or request changes when a finding blocks. The default |
| `comment` | A plain comment with the same findings. The bot never approves and never blocks, so it does not count toward required approvals and the merge is left to people |

### Round limit

**Reviews per pull request** stops the webhook after that many reviews. A request
obeys it too, and the skip reason reads `Round limit reached: 2 of 2 reviews.`
Leave it blank for no limit.

## Set it up

### In the dashboard

- **Repository settings**, card **Who gets a review.** Pick a template, read the
  plain sentences under **In short**, and open **Edit the rules** to change them.
  The sentences update as you edit, and **Save** is disabled while the policy is
  not valid. Editing a template turns it into custom rules.
- **Settings**, **Defaults for new repositories.** The template a repository
  starts with. Custom rules are set with a file, see below.
- **Add repository.** After the preview, the plan step lists the templates with
  their descriptions. The server default is selected, and you decide.

### On the command line

```sh
# The server default for new repositories
co-maintainer set --review-policy=trusted-auto

# A custom policy from a file
co-maintainer set --review-policy-file=policy.json

# Back to no default
co-maintainer set --unset=review-policy
```

A policy file is JSON. Everything except the rules can be left out:

```json
{
  "rules": [
    { "name": "draft", "when": { "draft": true }, "action": "skip" },
    {
      "name": "first time contributor",
      "when": { "association": ["FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR", "FIRST_TIMER"] },
      "action": "on-request"
    },
    {
      "name": "small change by anyone we know",
      "when": { "association": ["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR", "CONTRIBUTOR"], "changedLines": { "max": 300 } },
      "action": "review"
    }
  ],
  "default": "on-request",
  "requestLabel": "co-maintainer:review",
  "requestCommand": "/co-maintainer review",
  "requesters": ["OWNER", "MEMBER", "COLLABORATOR"],
  "approvalScope": "head",
  "maxRounds": 3
}
```

| Field | Values | Default |
| ----- | ------ | ------- |
| `rules[].action` and `default` | `review`, `on-request`, `skip` | `default` is `review` |
| `rules[].when` | `association`, `fork`, `draft`, `bot`, `labels`, `targetBranch`, `changedLines` (`min`, `max`) | No condition matches everything |
| `requestLabel` | Label name | `co-maintainer:review` |
| `requestCommand` | Text a comment starts with | `/co-maintainer review` |
| `requesters` | Author relations that may ask by comment | `OWNER`, `MEMBER`, `COLLABORATOR` |
| `skippers` | Author relations that may skip a failed review or turn reviews off, besides the owner | None |
| `approvalScope` | `head`, `pull-request` | `head` |
| `maxRounds` | Whole number of 1 or more | No limit |

A policy that cannot be read is refused and says what is wrong, for example
`unknown template "x"` or `rules[0].action must be one of review, on-request, skip`.
Nothing is saved.

## Existing repositories

A repository added before policies existed keeps the three switches it had:
automatic review on or off, skip drafts, skip bots. They behave exactly as they
always did, and the repository shows **Simple switches**. Choosing a template
replaces them. On a repository that follows a policy, the switches are hidden and
changing one through the API is refused with a message that says to change the
policy instead.

A new repository with no choice follows the server default. With no server
default it behaves like **Everyone**.

## Why a pull request was skipped

**Activity**, **Pull requests we skipped** names the rule that decided, for
example `Rule 3 (trusted author): waiting for a maintainer request.` or
`Default rule: waiting for a maintainer request.` A rule without a name shows its
position only, so name the rules you write.

## Permissions

A request needs nothing new. The eyes reaction uses the Issues permission the App
already has, and a label request arrives on the `pull_request` event it already
receives. See [GitHub App](github-app.md) for the permission table.

---

Source: https://co-maintainer.com/docs/local-pr-review.md

# PR review

Review an **open GitHub pull request** by number. The CLI uses **`gh`** to read
the PR and runs the AI **on your machine** with your [AI provider](providers.md).

Overview: [`review`](review.md). This is not the same as
[remote review](remote-review.md) (`--remote` is rejected when a PR number is
present).

Pushing straight to `main` without PRs: see
[commit watch review](commit-watch-review.md).

## Before you run

| Check | Why |
| ----- | --- |
| [`init`](init.md) / [`sync`](sync.md) for `owner/repo` | Guides on disk for that repo |
| `gh auth login` | PR review supports **`--auth=gh` only** |
| Read access to the PR | Private repos need a logged-in `gh` user |

## Usage

```sh
co-maintainer review owner/repo 123
co-maintainer review owner/repo 123 --json
co-maintainer review owner/repo 123 --fresh
co-maintainer review owner/repo 123 --disable-codegraph --debug
```

## Parameters

| Flag | Meaning |
| ------ | ----- |
| `owner/repo` | Repository (required positional) |
| `123` | Pull request number (required positional) |
| `--json` | One JSON document on stdout |
| `--fresh` | Ignore the stored run of this pull request and start over |
| `--disable-codegraph` | Skip codegraph tools (default is on for CLI) |
| `--allow-tool-install` | Install pinned codegraph without a prompt |
| `--improve-matrix=N` | Scales review depth (see CLI help) |
| `--intent-file=PATH` | What the change is for, from a file or `-` for standard input. Context only, read into the `PULL REQUEST` block, see [Intent](review.md#intent) |
| `--with=PATH[@BRANCH]` | Read a local checkout's changes as context, up to 5. The repository's `companions` setting adds [companion pull requests](companions.md#companion-pull-requests), and `--with` wins for a repository given both ways |
| `--diagram-runtime`, `--plantuml-server`, `--plantuml-output-format` | The diagram language of the review, see [Diagrams](review.md#diagrams) |
| `--include-extension-markdowns` | With `--json`, keep each extension's Markdown, which is empty otherwise |
| `--debug` | Verbose logs on stderr |
| `--log-time` | Print timing per phase |

Registered [extensions](extensions.md) run in a PR review too, and their findings
join the result. The extension makes its own checkout if it needs one.

**Not supported for PR review:** `--remote`, `--to-branch`, `--branch`,
`--repo=`, `--sync-before-review`. Use
[local review](local-review.md) for working-tree changes or
[remote review](remote-review.md) for a local diff against shared server context.

PR review indexes the checked-out repository with codegraph when it is already
installed, and installs the pinned version when you pass `--allow-tool-install`.
It never prompts: a PR review runs unattended. The question and its rules are in
[local review](local-review.md#codegraph), and [Codegraph](codegraph.md) lists
the install table and the version-resolution order.

Auth and models follow [`configuration`](configuration.md) and `co-maintainer
set` like other commands. PR review reads GitHub through `gh`: a saved
`auth=pat` is left out and the review goes on with `gh`, and `--auth=pat` on
the command line is refused.

## Carry-over

A PR review remembers its findings between runs. Each run is stored in the
[cache](caching.md), keyed by repository and pull request number. The next run
shows what the author fixed as `closed`, what is left as `open`, and only real
new findings as `new`. This is the same carry-over [local review](local-review.md#carry-over)
uses, and it shows in the terminal output, in `--json` and with `--output=github`.

- **Starts fresh** with `--fresh`, when the guide was rebuilt after the last run,
  and when the pull request head does not contain the last reviewed head. That is
  a force-push, or a case where GitHub cannot compare the two. Starting fresh
  clears the stored run, and the log says why.
- **Unchanged files** since the last run are listed to the model as unchanged
  and are not sent again. A re-run on the same head sends no file, still makes
  one model call to judge the earlier findings, and every finding comes back
  `open`. A re-run after a push sends only the changed files.
- **Exit code.** A blocking finding that is still open keeps the exit code at 1,
  also when the model reports nothing new.
- **A cache problem never fails the review.** If the stored run cannot be read or
  saved, the review runs without carry-over and the output carries a
  `carry_over_unavailable` warning.
- **`clear owner/repo --include-cache`** removes the stored runs, see
  [Caching](caching.md#clearing).

A file the model did not receive because the diff was too large is sent again in
the next run, see [Large diffs](review.md#large-diffs).

In `--json`, `summary.open` and `summary.closed` count the findings, each
`findings[].state` is `new`, `open` or `closed`, and `warnings` holds
`carry_over_unavailable` and the [large diff](review.md#where-the-result-says-it)
warnings.

---

Source: https://co-maintainer.com/docs/commit-watch-review.md

# Commit watch review

Review pushes to your default branch when there is no pull request. It is a
sub-page of [PR review](local-pr-review.md), for the case where PR review
cannot apply.

## Why

If you push straight to `main` and do not use branches or pull requests,
nothing gets reviewed. [PR review](local-pr-review.md) needs a PR, so it never
runs for you.

## Turn it on

Commit watch is a feature of [`serve`](serve.md). The repository must be added
and initialized on the server. On the repository's **Pushes** tab in the
[dashboard](dashboard.md), the **Commit watch** card shows whether pushes are
watched and the two ways to turn it on. The overview keeps a short status line
that links there. Use either one, or both.

**GitHub App.** In the App's settings on GitHub open **Permissions & events**
and tick **Push** under **Subscribe to events**. That is your explicit yes, and
it applies to every repository the App is installed on. The App watches the
default branch only. See [GitHub App](github-app.md).

**CI.** Add a workflow that runs the co-maintainer action on a push. The card
gives you the workflow with your server's address filled in. See
[CI](ci.md#review-pushes-commit-watch).

When both report the same push, it is reviewed once and the CI step waits for
that review.

`co-maintainer probe` shows a `commit watch` line when the machine it runs on
has the GitHub App configured.

## How a push is reviewed

One push is reviewed as a single diff, from the commit before the push to the
commit after it. It is not reviewed commit by commit. A push that merges a pull
request is reviewed too.

- A push that creates the branch has nothing to compare with, so it is not
  reviewed.
- After a force-push or a rebase, open issues stay and the new commits are
  reviewed.
- Only pushes after you turn it on are reviewed. History is not scanned, and a
  push the server missed while it was down is not reviewed later.
- A repository that is not initialized is not reviewed. With the App, the
  commit gets a skipped check run that says so. With CI and no App, the step
  fails.
- A push review runs no [extensions](extensions.md).
- A push with a very large diff is reviewed within the diff budget. A push review
  does not carry its seen files into the next push, so files that did not fit are
  dropped again, and the review's warning says so. See
  [Large diffs](review.md#large-diffs).

When pushes come in a row, the repository settings decide what happens:

| Setting | What happens |
| ------- | ------------ |
| Review each push in turn (default) | Every push gets its own review, oldest first. |
| Cancel and merge into the newest | A waiting or running review is canceled and its range is reviewed together with the newest push. |

## It never blocks you

The push is already in, so a finding never fails anything.

- **With the App** the commit gets a check run that always succeeds, with the
  findings as annotations.
- **With CI** findings are warnings and the step stays green. After the
  `timeout-minutes` input (10 by default) the step ends green with a notice,
  and the review finishes on the server. The step fails only when it cannot
  reach the server or the token is refused.

Every push review, its findings by severity and its cost are on the
**Pushes** tab of the repository.

## Issues for P0 and P1

Each P0 and P1 finding becomes a GitHub issue. Issues are opened by the GitHub
App, so without the App there are none. It is on by default and can be turned
off per repository in its settings. P2 and P3 findings are annotations and on
the dashboard only.

An issue is titled `[P1] <what is wrong>` and labeled `co-maintainer` and
`cm-P1` (the labels are created when missing). The body says where the problem
is, with a link to the code at the pushed commit, and which push found it.
Issues are written in English.

The server keeps track of each issue, and a finding with the same file and code
as an earlier one is not opened again.

### When the code changes

A push that changes the lines of an open issue's finding gets a comment, and
the review is asked about that issue explicitly:

- Still there: `change in <commit> (push <after>): changed, still found by the
  review of <range>`. When the commit is the push, its hash is written once.
- Fixed: `change in <commit>: changed, no longer found by the review of
  <range>. Closing.`, and co-maintainer closes the issue. It closes an issue
  only when a push changed those lines and the review said that problem is
  fixed. If it is not allowed to close issues, it says so in a comment.

### When you close an issue yourself

The first push review after you close it checks the problem once, even when the
push does not touch that file. If the problem is still there, co-maintainer
says so on the same issue and asks you to leave a comment if there is something
it should know. The issue stays closed, and it says this once per closing.

If that review finds it solved and the problem comes back later, a new issue is
opened.

### Talking to it on an issue

co-maintainer reads comments on the issues it opened, from people with write
access, and only when the comment is meant for it. "@someone can you take a
look" is not.

- A question gets an answer, in the language of the question.
- A comment that says to ignore the finding, or that tells it something, gets
  "Noted, I will take this into account on the next sync." The next
  [sync](sync.md) adds the note to the detailed review guide, and a finding you
  said to ignore is not reported, commented on or opened as an issue again.

---

Source: https://co-maintainer.com/docs/extensions.md

# Extensions

An extension is a command you register. co-maintainer runs it around a
review, reads one JSON document from its stdout, and joins its findings,
verdict, Markdown and cost into the review. Nothing is built in. Any check
can plug in without changing co-maintainer: a linter, a secret scanner, a
browser QA run that records videos.

Extensions run in every review type: a [local review](local-review.md), a
[PR review](local-pr-review.md) from the CLI, the reviews
[`serve`](serve.md) posts as the [GitHub App](github-app.md), and a
[remote review](remote-review.md), where `serve` runs the extensions
registered on `serve`. A [commit watch](commit-watch-review.md) push review runs
none.

## Register one

```sh
co-maintainer extension register --name=qa-vision \
  --command='HOME=/home/me /usr/bin/node /opt/qa-vision.mjs {{details_path}} --json'
co-maintainer extension debug-run --name=qa-vision
co-maintainer extension list
```

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- | ------- |
| `--name` | required | The extension's name, its id in every output |
| `--command` | required | The shell command, with `{{variable}}` paths |
| `--repos` | `*` | `owner/repo`, `a/b,a/c`, `a/*`, `*/a` |
| `--review-types` | all | `local`, `pr`, `remote`, comma separated |
| `--run-after` | none | An extension name, or `review` |
| `--parallelism=true\|false` | `true` | `false` with no `--run-after` runs after the review |
| `--priority` | `0` | `0` to `3`, 3 starts first, ties keep registration order |
| `--fail-fast` | off | On failure, what waits on it through `--run-after` does not run |
| `--retry-on-fail-times` | `0` | Runs again when the response does not match the schema |
| `--max-requested-retries` | `3` | How many `status: retry` responses are honoured |
| `--timeout` | `10m` | Such as `30s`, `10m` or `1h`, at most `6h` |
| `--rerun-on-restart=true\|false` | `true` | Overrides the `extension-rerun-on-restart` config key |

The dashboard manages them too, under **Settings**, **Extensions**: the list,
**Register**, **Enable** or **Disable**, and **Remove**. It runs the same
checks as the CLI, so a value one side refuses the other refuses too. A
run-after name nobody registered is saved there without asking, as `--yes`
does.

`update` takes the same flags and changes only the ones given. `remove`,
`disable` and `enable` take `--name`. Registrations live in `config.json` as an
`extensions` array, and the array order is the registration order.

`register` and `update` refuse a `--run-after` cycle. A `--run-after` name that
nobody registered asks "Are you sure?" first. Without a terminal, pass `--yes`.

## The command

co-maintainer runs your command through `/bin/sh -c` (`cmd /d /s /c` on Windows) and
replaces three variables with quoted paths:

| Variable | What it points at |
| -------- | ----------------- |
| `{{details_path}}` | `details.json`, the review's context |
| `{{review_result_path}}` | `cm-review.json`, the AI review's findings. Empty for an extension that starts before the review finishes |
| `{{diff_path}}` | `diff.patch`, the unified diff, in every review type |

Write a variable bare, `{{details_path}}`, never inside your own quotes. Only
paths are substituted, so nothing a pull request author wrote, such as a
branch name or a title, ever reaches the shell. Any other `{{name}}` is
refused when you register.

The command starts with an empty environment. No token or key co-maintainer
holds is passed to it. Set what the command needs inside the command itself,
`HOME=/home/me /usr/bin/node ...`, and use absolute paths. Credentials in a
command are the extension's responsibility, and so is checking out or running
pull request code.

The command runs as the user that runs co-maintainer, `serve` included, and
can read every file that user can read. That includes `config.json`, which
holds co-maintainer's keys. An extension that runs pull request code must
sandbox that code itself. Outside a local review the command runs in its run
folder.

The three files sit in one folder per review, shared by its extensions:

```
<config dir>/co-maintainer/extensions/<run-id>/details.json
<config dir>/co-maintainer/extensions/<run-id>/cm-review.json
<config dir>/co-maintainer/extensions/<run-id>/diff.patch
```

With `CM_CONFIG_PATH` set, the run folders live in
`co-maintainer-extensions` next to that `config.json` instead.

The folder is removed however the review ends. `serve` removes the folders of
jobs no longer running when it starts, and the CLI removes those of runs whose
process is gone on its next review.

### details.json

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "reviewType": "pr",
  "repo": "owner/repo",
  "prNumber": 45,
  "branch": "feature",
  "workdir": "",
  "headSha": "4f1c2d9a...",
  "baseSha": "9a8b7c6d...",
  "scope": "incremental",
  "sinceCommit": "1e2d3c4b...",
  "trigger": "synchronize",
  "round": 2,
  "reviewResultPath": "",
  "diffPath": "/home/me/.config/co-maintainer/extensions/9f.../diff.patch"
}
```

In a local review `prNumber` is null, `branch` and `workdir` are set, and the
command runs in `workdir`. In a PR review and in `serve`, `workdir` is empty
and the extension makes its own checkout if it needs one. A remote review has
no `workdir` either, because the checkout is on the client's machine.
`reviewResultPath` is filled in once the AI review has finished.

`cm-review.json` holds `schemaVersion`, `summary` and `findings`, in the same
finding shape `review --json` prints.

## The response

Print exactly one JSON document on stdout. Log lines go to stderr.

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "name": "qa-vision",
  "status": "ok",
  "verdict": "request_changes",
  "markdown": "**QA vision (beta)** found one problem.",
  "findings": [
    {
      "key": "snapshot-button",
      "severity": "P2",
      "blocking": true,
      "title": "Snapshot button missing",
      "body": "The toolbar hides the button while a snapshot runs.",
      "path": "src/snapshot/toolbar.tsx",
      "lineFrom": 15,
      "lineTo": 21
    }
  ],
  "data": {
    "media": [{ "kind": "video", "label": "main", "url": "https://cdn.example.com/main.mp4" }],
    "metrics": [{ "name": "cases", "value": 4 }]
  },
  "extraData": { "cases": [] },
  "usage": { "costUsd": 0.42, "tokensIn": 0, "tokensOut": 0 }
}
```

<!-- extension-schema:start -->
| Field | Type | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `schemaVersion` | integer | yes | Must be 1. Any other value is Failed, with that as the reason. |
| `name` | string | yes | The extension's own name, for its logs. (at most 100 characters) |
| `status` | `ok`, `failed`, `skipped`, `retry` | yes | How the run ended. |
| `verdict` | `request_changes`, `comment` | with `ok`, absent otherwise | `request_changes` makes the whole review Request changes. It always wins over a finding's `blocking`. |
| `reason` | string | with `skipped` and `retry` | Why the extension skipped, failed or wants a retry. (at most 2000 characters) |
| `retryAfterSeconds` | integer | with `retry` | How long to wait before the next run. (min 0, max 180) |
| `markdown` | string | no | Shown in the GitHub review and the job summary, inside a `<details>` block named after the extension. (at most 200000 characters) |
| `findings` | array of objects | no | Findings that join the review. |
| `findings[].key` | string | no | A stable id. With one, the finding is tracked across rounds: seen again means still open, missing means closed. (at most 200 characters) |
| `findings[].severity` | `P0`, `P1`, `P2`, `P3` | yes | P0 is the most severe. |
| `findings[].blocking` | boolean | yes | Whether this finding alone should block the merge. |
| `findings[].title` | string | yes | One line. (at most 500 characters) |
| `findings[].body` | string | yes | The explanation, in Markdown. (at most 20000 characters) |
| `findings[].path` | string | no | A file path relative to the repository root. (at most 1000 characters) |
| `findings[].lineFrom` | integer | no | First line in the new file. (min 1) |
| `findings[].lineTo` | integer | no | Last line in the new file. (min 1) |
| `data` | object | no | Results with a fixed shape co-maintainer can show. |
| `data.media` | array of objects | no | Files the extension uploaded itself. co-maintainer uploads nothing. |
| `data.media[].kind` | `image`, `video`, `link` | yes | What the URL points at. |
| `data.media[].label` | string | yes | A short name, such as `main` or `pr`. (at most 100 characters) |
| `data.media[].url` | string (URL) | yes | An http or https URL. |
| `data.metrics` | array of objects | no | Numbers worth showing next to the result. |
| `data.metrics[].name` | string | yes | What was measured. |
| `data.metrics[].value` | number | yes | The measurement. |
| `data.metrics[].unit` | string | no | Such as `ms` or `MB`. |
| `extraData` | any | no | Free-form. Passed through to `--json` and never read by co-maintainer. |
| `usage` | object | no | What the run cost, when it used AI. |
| `usage.costUsd` | number | no | Joins the review's total cost. (min 0, max 10000) |
| `usage.tokensIn` | integer | no | Input tokens. (min 0, max 10000000000) |
| `usage.tokensOut` | integer | no | Output tokens. (min 0, max 10000000000) |
| `usage.cachedIn` | integer | no | Cached input tokens. (min 0, max 10000000000) |
| `usage.cachedOut` | integer | no | Cached output tokens. (min 0, max 10000000000) |
<!-- extension-schema:end -->

- Unknown fields are ignored.
- An unsupported `schemaVersion` is Failed, with that as the reason.
- A response that does not match the schema is Failed. With
  `--retry-on-fail-times`, the command runs again first.
- `retry` waits `retryAfterSeconds` and runs the command again, up to
  `--max-requested-retries` times. After that the result is Failed.
- Each attempt gets the full `--timeout`. The longest an extension can take is
  one attempt, plus `--retry-on-fail-times` attempts, plus
  `--max-requested-retries` attempts with their waits.
- Inside the `<details>` block, `details` and `summary` tags in `markdown` are
  shown as text, and a heading named like one of the review's own sections is
  escaped. Mentions and images are posted as written: the extension owner is
  responsible for them, even when a pull request shaped them.
- Media is always a URL the extension uploaded itself. co-maintainer uploads
  nothing.

## Order and failures

- The AI review is the start point and never waits for an extension or reads
  its output. The review is posted only after every extension has finished.
- Extensions run on every review, incremental ones included. There is no
  trigger filter: `details.json` has the fields to decide, and an extension can
  return `skipped`.
- A `--run-after` target that does not exist, or does not run for this review,
  skips the extension that waits on it. So does a target that returns
  `skipped`.
- A `--fail-fast` failure skips what waits on it. Extensions not connected to
  it are not affected.
- A timeout or a cancel sends SIGTERM to the command's process group and
  SIGKILL 30 seconds later. The result is Failed.
- When co-maintainer restarts while an extension runs, the extension runs
  again. With `--rerun-on-restart=false` the result is Failed instead.
- Failures do not block. A failed extension is named in the summary and its
  reason, with stdout and stderr and the exit code (at most 128 KB), is kept
  for the dashboard.

## What the review shows

- One extension's `request_changes` makes the whole review Request changes
  and the CLI exit code blocking (1). A verdict always wins over a finding's
  own `blocking`.
- Any other extension finding is non-blocking. It stays a comment and never
  holds back the App's approval.
- In the GitHub review, a finding on a diff line is posted inline, headed
  `[P2 · blocking] · extension: name`. A finding off the diff, or with no
  location, goes in the summary list with the same label. At most 50
  extension comments go inline and 50 findings are listed, then a line says
  how many more the dashboard holds.
- An `#### Extensions` section follows the review summary, with each
  extension's `markdown` inside a `<details>` block. The whole review body is
  capped at 250,000 characters. Over it, the longest `markdown` is replaced
  with "Not added to this comment because of the length limit, see the
  dashboard.", then the next longest, until it fits. The AI review is never
  cut.
- Metadata lists `Extensions`, `Failed Extensions`, `Skipped Extensions` and
  `Requested changes`.
- The terminal shows each extension's findings and `data`, never its
  `markdown`.
- `review --json` adds `extensions[]` and puts extension findings into
  `findings[]` with `extensionId`. AI findings have `extensionId: null`.
  `markdown` is empty unless you pass `--include-extension-markdowns`.
- `review --output=github` annotates located findings with the extension
  label, within the 10 per level GitHub shows, and the job summary lists all
  of them with each `markdown`. The job summary is capped at 1 MiB, by the
  same longest first rule.
- The dashboard shows each result with its fail or skip reason.

A finding with a `key` is tracked across rounds: seen again means still open,
missing means closed. A finding without a `key` is shown fresh each run and
never closed.

The total cost of a review includes its extensions. The review's own cost is
the total minus the extensions, and each extension's cost comes from its
`usage`.

## Try it with debug-run

`co-maintainer extension debug-run --name=NAME` runs one extension against a
built-in mock of pull request 45 of `GroophyLifefor/heap-analysis`: its
context, its diff and a finished AI review. There is no AI call, no network
and nothing is posted. Pass `--command=...` to try a command before you
register it. The run prints what the terminal output of a review would show,
and the full output when the extension failed.

## Turning extensions off

`CM_EXTENSIONS_DISABLED=1` turns extensions off. `register` and `debug-run`
refuse, and no review runs an extension. The hosted cloud sets it from
outside the container, so extensions are always off there. On a self-hosted
Docker image, tools an extension needs, such as ffmpeg or a browser, are for
the extension owner to add with their own image.

## Changing the schema

This part is for people changing co-maintainer itself.

- The response schema lives in `src/extensions/schema.ts` as one list of
  field specs. The validator reads it, and the table on this page is generated
  from it. `npm run docs:build` rewrites the table, and a test fails when the
  table here is older than the code.
- Adding an optional field, or a new value an extension may send, keeps
  `schemaVersion` at 1. Old extensions keep working because unknown fields
  are ignored.
- Removing a field, renaming one, making one required, or changing what a
  value means is a new `schemaVersion`. An extension built for a version this
  build does not read gets Failed with that reason, so the reason tells its
  owner what to change.
- `details.json` follows the same rules with its own `schemaVersion`.

---

Source: https://co-maintainer.com/docs/companions.md

# Companions

Some changes span repositories: code and its docs, or a backend and the editor
extension that calls it. A review sees one repository's diff, so it cannot tell
whether the other side changed in step, or did not change at all.

A companion is another repository's change for the same task, read as
context. A companion is read, never reviewed, and needs no `init`. The reviewed
change keeps its whole diff budget. There are two ways to name one:

- **`--with`** points a review at another checkout on your machine. It works in
  [local review](local-review.md), [PR review](local-pr-review.md) and
  [remote review](remote-review.md).
- **Companion pull requests** link pull requests that belong together. They work
  in [App review](github-app.md) and [PR review](local-pr-review.md), see
  [Companion pull requests](#companion-pull-requests).

```sh
co-maintainer review --with=../docs
co-maintainer review --with=../docs --with=../vscode-ext@feature/session-api --intent-file=task.md
co-maintainer review owner/repo 42 --with=../docs
co-maintainer review --remote --with=../vscode-ext@feature/session-api
```

## The flag

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--with=PATH[@BRANCH]` | none | A companion checkout. Repeat it for each companion, up to 5 |

- **Without `@BRANCH`** the companion's current branch and working tree are
  read, the same way local review reads its own checkout: committed, staged,
  unstaged and untracked changes against the merge base with its default
  branch.
- **With `@BRANCH`** that branch is diffed against its merge base with the
  companion's default branch. The checkout is never switched, and its working
  tree is not read. A local branch is tried first, then the remote's.
- **The repository name** comes from the companion's git remote, `upstream`
  first, then `origin`. Only GitHub remotes work, as in local review.
- **A folder with `@` in its name** works: a value that names a folder is a
  path whole. Otherwise the text after the last `@` is the branch.
- **Not with `--range`.** A push review takes no companions.

Every error is a usage error with exit code 2, before any model call:

| Case | Message |
| --- | --- |
| PATH is not a git repository | `--with: PATH is not a git repository` |
| BRANCH does not exist there | `--with: no branch BRANCH in owner/repo` |
| PATH is the repository under review | `--with: PATH is the repository under review` |
| More than 5 companions | `--with: at most 5 companions` |
| The same repository twice | `--with: owner/repo is given more than once` |
